title: The Poll Demand
scenario: Chairperson: “At our 80-lot Standard Module scheme’s AGM, owners considered 5 motions in identical form, each approving a separate $3,200 garden maintenance quote for a different section of common property. After the show of hands on the first motion, an eligible owner called for a poll. She says the poll should cover all 5 motions together, because they are the same motion repeated. I say each motion needs its own poll.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about the poll request?”
modelAnswer: Let her have her poll, and run it once for all five. Five identical motions don't need five identical rituals. Once a poll is called, the show of hands is dead. Voters mark a single paper, a yes or no on each motion, and every motion still wins or loses on its own count. Refuse, or drag out five separate polls, and you've handed her a reason to challenge the whole meeting.
markingGuide: Best answer is the one that is clear, sharp and memorable, not the longest. It should: allow the poll; use one poll for the group of same-form motions; keep each motion's result separate. Bonus for a vivid line that makes the point stick.

title: Coin Flip
scenario: Candidate B: “At our Standard Module scheme’s AGM, the chair accepted 3 floor votes from a proxyholder representing 3 lot owners. The count for Chair came out 20–20 between me and Candidate A. The strata manager assisting the meeting immediately announced the tie would be decided by chance, flipped a coin, and declared Candidate A the winner.”
instructions: “What legal advice would you give Candidate B about the validity of this election process and the outcome?”
modelAnswer: A tie can be settled by chance, so the coin isn't the problem. The problem is who called it. The meeting decides how chance is used, not the strata manager, and the manager only assists the chair. Then there's the count: committee elections run by ballot, so 3 floor votes from a proxyholder are doubtful. If they shouldn't have counted, there was never a tie. Object, get it minuted, collect the ballots, proxies and minutes, write to the body corporate, and get proper legal advice before escalating.
markingGuide: Best answer is the one that is clear, sharp and memorable, not the longest. It should: accept that chance is a valid way to break a tie; spot that the meeting, not the strata manager, decides the method and the chair runs the election; question whether the proxy floor votes were valid in a ballot election; give practical steps (object, get it minuted, get the papers, write to the body corporate, seek legal advice). Bonus for a vivid line that makes the point stick.

title: The Transfer in Transit
scenario: Chairperson: “At our Standard Module scheme’s AGM, an owner owed 4 months of levies. She tells me she transferred the full amount from her bank this morning, but she has nothing to show me. Our bank hasn’t confirmed any money has arrived. She votes against an ordinary motion to repaint the stairwells. Without her vote it carries 12 to 11. I ruled her vote out because she owes levies, and declared the motion carried. We later find out she had paid.”
instructions: “What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson about her vote?”
modelAnswer: This one is grey, and the best answer says so. The test is whether she owes at the time of voting. Her word isn't proof, and an empty bank screen isn't proof either. So don't decide on say-so. Ask her for bank proof on the spot and check the body corporate's account. If she can show the money was sent and it lands, her vote should have counted: it's 12 all and the motion fails. If nothing can be shown, the rule stands, but record her vote as disputed so the result can be fixed. A one-vote margin is no place for a guess.
markingGuide: Best answer is the one that is clear, sharp and memorable, not the longest. It should: identify that the test is whether she owes levies at the time of voting; recognise this is a grey area (paid but not yet received, and no proof at the meeting); advise getting proof or checking the account rather than ruling on assumption; note that counting her vote makes it 12 all and the motion fails; suggest recording her vote as disputed if it can't be confirmed. Bonus for a vivid line that makes the point stick.

title: The Fee Blowout
scenario: A scheme’s fee-for-service (FFS) charges finished the financial year at 200% of budget. Most of the overrun came from a long legal dispute with lot buyers, who relied on an unregistered community management statement (CMS) that gave the wrong carpark allocations. The treasurer asks the community manager to explain the FFS total. Going through the ledger, the manager finds several entries with next to no description. Together they make up about 3% of the FFS charges.
instructions: What should the community manager do?
topic: Fee for service charges and transparency
modelAnswer: Don't dodge it, and don't tidy it. The treasurer asked for an explanation, so give one. Break the FFS down by matter: dispute work on one side, routine work on the other. That shows where the 200% came from. Then raise the thin entries yourself before the treasurer finds them. Three per cent is small, but unexplained charges make the other 97% look shaky. Check each one against what the body corporate actually authorised (the engagement agreement or a committee instruction) and the backup: instruction, timesheet, invoice. Anything that stacks up gets a proper description. Anything that doesn't gets credited. Never go back and rewrite a description to make an entry look better. Fix it with a credit, not a better story.
markingGuide: Best answer is the one that is clear, sharp and memorable, not the longest. It should: give the treasurer a real explanation by splitting the FFS between the dispute and routine work; raise the unexplained entries openly rather than leave them or hope they pass; check each against the authority to do the work and the backup (instruction, timesheet, invoice); credit or correct anything that can't be supported; and not alter or embellish records after the fact. Don't mark down for mentioning that the overrun was or wasn't authorised, but the core is honesty and substantiating the charges. Bonus for a vivid line that makes the point stick.

title: Paint Over It
scenario: Azure Heights. Lot 804 reports a brown spot on the ceiling, twice. Each time the committee chair says, “Paint over it and see.” Then a flexi hose bursts in the unit above, floods two floors and takes out the lift. The chair now wants to know why the strata manager “didn’t escalate it properly”.
instructions: How do you respond to the chair, and what steps do you take now to manage the insurance claim and work out who pays?
topic: Water damage, insurance claims and responsibility
modelAnswer:
Answer the chair with facts, not a fight. Pull the file and lay out the timeline: when each report came in, what you recommended, and the chair's instruction each time. Say it plainly and without blame: the reports were passed on and the committee's direction was to paint and monitor. Don't rewrite history and don't point fingers. Offer what you would do differently next time, such as a written recommendation for an inspection and a record of the committee's decision to defer. Tell your own office to notify your professional indemnity insurer if the chair is hinting at a claim against you.

Then run the claim. Make the building safe first: stop the water, isolate power to the lift and affected areas, and get emergency repairs under way. Notify the body corporate's insurer straight away, and your broker, before anything is thrown out. Keep the burst hose and fittings as evidence, take photos, and don't let anyone dispose of them. Tell all affected owners in writing, and ask each to notify their own contents insurer. Keep the earlier ceiling reports and the chair's instructions on the claim file, because the insurer will ask about prior warnings.

Who pays comes down to cause and responsibility. The body corporate's policy generally responds to the building damage, and it carries the excess. The hose sits inside the unit above, so look at whether the owner of that lot is responsible, whether through their own negligence or lack of maintenance, and whether their insurer should be put on notice. Don't promise recovery to anyone. Get the loss adjuster's findings, check the policy for exclusions such as gradual leakage or lack of maintenance, and get advice before the committee decides how to allocate the excess or pursue the owner.
markingGuide: Best answer is the one that is clear, sharp and memorable, not the longest. It should: respond to the chair calmly with a factual timeline from the records, not defensiveness or blame; make the building safe and notify the insurer and broker immediately; preserve the burst hose and photograph the damage; notify affected owners and ask them to tell their own insurers; hand over the earlier ceiling reports and the chair's instructions honestly, because the insurer will ask about prior warnings; look at the responsibility of the lot owner above and whether their insurer should be put on notice; and avoid promising who pays before the loss adjuster and policy wording are known. Credit mentioning the strata manager's own professional indemnity notification. Don't mark down for different wording on the excess, but mark down anyone who alters records, hides the earlier reports or guesses at liability. Bonus for a vivid line that makes the point stick.

title: The Poll Tolls for Thee!
scenario: At our 65-lot Standard Module scheme’s AGM, we reached a contentious motion to approve a $95,000 external painting contract. Before the chairperson even called for a show of hands, a corporate owner holding 12 lots stood up and demanded we go straight to a poll to save time. Another owner objected, saying we have to do a show of hands first. Who is right?
instructions: What should the body corporate manager advise the chairperson?
modelAnswer:
The corporate owner is right. Go straight to the poll. A poll can be demanded by any person entitled to vote, and it can be demanded whether or not the meeting has already voted on the motion. So there is no rule that a show of hands must come first, and the objecting owner is wrong. The chairperson can't refuse or insist on a show of hands first. Check the person demanding it is entitled to vote, then run it.

The advice to the chair: don't argue the point, accept the demand and explain what happens next. A poll replaces the show of hands, so the show of hands is skipped. Voters mark a paper and the count is by contribution schedule lot entitlements, not one vote per lot. The motion passes only if the entitlements of the yes lots exceed those of the no lots. That matters here, because the result could differ from a count of hands, and the owner with 12 lots may carry real weight. The demand can be withdrawn by the person who made it, but only before the poll is finished.

Also keep the meeting clean on a $95,000 contract: the motion should be in the notice, the quotes should be before the meeting, and the minutes should record that a poll was demanded, who demanded it, and the result. Refuse it, or do a show of hands first and then try to block the poll, and you've handed the losing side a reason to challenge the whole decision.
markingGuide: Best answer is the one that is clear, sharp and memorable, not the longest. It should: say plainly that the corporate owner is right and the show of hands is not required first; explain that a poll can be demanded by anyone entitled to vote, whether or not a show of hands has happened; advise the chairperson to accept the demand and not refuse or delay it; explain that a poll counts contribution schedule lot entitlements, not one vote per lot, so the result can differ; and record the demand and the result in the minutes. Credit checking the person demanding is entitled to vote. Mark down anyone who says a show of hands must come first, or who lets the chair refuse the poll. Don't mark down for leaving out section numbers. Bonus for a vivid line that makes the point stick.
